title: The rules every probability obeys
objectives: State the axioms and derive simple consequences from them.
Use monotonicity and the union bound to test whether stated chances are consistent.

screens.title: Which numbers could be chances?
screens.prose: Four pundits give chances for tomorrow's match. Exactly one result will happen: a home win, a draw or an away win.

state.caption: Exactly one of the three results will happen

screens.question: Tap every pundit whose numbers could be real probabilities.

hints.text: Add each pundit's three numbers. What must they add to?
Also look for a number no chance can be.
Ben adds to 1.1 and Dee to 0.6. Cal adds to 1, but one of Cal's chances is negative.

feedback.correct: Only Ana's numbers are all at least 0 and add to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check two things in each row: the sum, and the sign of each number.

byKey.r1: Ben's chances add to 1.1. The three results cover everything exactly once, so they must add to 1.
byKey.r2: Cal's add to 1, but an away win gets −0.1. No chance can be negative.
byKey.r3: Dee's add to 0.6. One result is certain to happen, so the three must add to 1.
byKey.r0: Ana's row passes both checks: no negatives, and a total of 1.

explain.text: Ana's numbers are all at least 0 and add to 1. Ben's add to 1.1 and Dee's to 0.6, but something certain must have chance 1. Cal's add to 1, yet a chance of −0.1 means nothing.

screens.prose: Build your own forecast. Move the home win and draw sliders. The away win gets whatever is left, so the three always add to 1.

derive.caption: Away win gets what is left: {{fixed(1 - values.home - values.draw, 2)}}

screens.question: With the home win at 0.55, what is the largest chance the draw can have?

hints.text: Push the draw up and watch the away bar.
The away bar must not go below 0.
Away is $1 - 0.55 - \text{draw}$, so the draw can reach $0.45$.

feedback.correct: A draw of 0.45 leaves the away win at exactly 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise the draw until the away bar would dip below zero.

byKey.whole: A draw of 1 leaves the away win at −0.55. No chance can be negative.
byKey.same: A draw of 0.55 pushes the away win to −0.1, below zero.
byKey.half: You split what is left evenly. The draw can take all of it if the away win gets 0.

explain.text: With the home win at 0.55, the draw and away win share 0.45. The away bar cannot go below zero, so the draw tops out at 0.45. Two rules did the work: the total is 1, and nothing is negative.

screens.title: The three axioms
screens.prose:
You used rules that every probability obeys. They are the **axioms**, for a sample space $S$:
1. $P(S) = 1$.
2. $P(E) \ge 0$ for every event $E$.
3. If $E_1, E_2, \dots$ are disjoint, $P(E_1 \cup E_2 \cup \cdots) = P(E_1) + P(E_2) + \cdots$.

We mostly use axiom 3 for two events. The dart example later needs the infinite list: all the fractions in $[0, 1]$ together get $0 + 0 + \cdots = 0$.
screens.question: Using Ana's forecast, what is the chance the home side does not lose?

widget.label: Chance the home side does not lose

hints.text: Not losing means a home win or a draw.
A home win and a draw cannot both happen, so they are disjoint.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the results where the home side does not lose, then use axiom 3.

byKey.home: That is a home win only. A draw is also not a loss.
byKey.product: You multiplied. The results are disjoint, so their chances add.
byKey.away: That is the chance the home side loses. You want the rest.

explain.text: A home win and a draw are disjoint, so axiom 3 adds them: $0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8$. The complement gives the same: $1 - 0.2 = 0.8$. We derive that complement rule next.

screens.title: The empty event
screens.prose: The empty event $\emptyset$ contains no outcomes. Show from the axioms that $P(\emptyset) = 0$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $S$ and $\emptyset$ share no outcome, so they are disjoint, and $S \cup \emptyset = S$.
The left side is $P(S)$, so $P(S) = P(S) + P(\emptyset)$.

hints.text: Axiom 3 needs two disjoint events. Which two?
Use $S$ and $\emptyset$ themselves.
Disjoint first, then axiom 3, then replace $S \cup \emptyset$ by $S$, then subtract.

feedback.correct: Each line uses only the axioms and the line before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the events are disjoint before using axiom 3.

byKey.s2: Axiom 3 applies only once you know the events are disjoint. Show that first.

explain.text: Adding the empty event to $S$ changes nothing, yet axiom 3 adds $P(\emptyset)$. The only way both hold is $P(\emptyset) = 0$. No counting was needed.

screens.title: The complement rule
screens.prose: Now derive the complement rule from the axioms. One line of the chain is missing. $$\begin{aligned} &E \text{ and } E^c \text{ are disjoint, and } E \cup E^c = S. \\ &\text{Axiom 3: } P(E) + P(E^c) = P(E \cup E^c). \\ &\text{[missing]} \\ &\text{So } P(E^c) = 1 - P(E). \end{aligned}$$
screens.question: Which line fills the gap?

options.text: $P(E \cup E^c) = P(S) = 1$, by axiom 1.
$P(E \cap E^c) = 0$, since the events are disjoint.
options.why: That is true, but it says nothing about the sum on the right.

options.text: $P(E^c) \ge 0$, by axiom 2.
options.why: That is true, but it does not turn $P(E \cup E^c)$ into a number.

options.text: $P(E) = P(E^c) = \tfrac{1}{2}$, by symmetry.
options.why: Nothing makes $E$ and $E^c$ equally likely. A die gives $P(\text{six}) = \tfrac{1}{6}$.

hints.text: The last line has a 1 in it. Where can a 1 come from?
$E \cup E^c$ is the whole sample space.
Axiom 1 says $P(S) = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gap must turn $P(E \cup E^c)$ into a number.

byKey.pos: That is true, but it does not turn $P(E \cup E^c)$ into a number.

explain.text: Since $E \cup E^c = S$, axiom 1 makes the sum equal to 1. Rearranging gives $P(E^c) = 1 - P(E)$. Add axiom 2, $P(E^c) \ge 0$, and we get $P(E) \le 1$ for free.

screens.title: Bigger events are more likely
screens.prose: Suppose $A \subseteq B$: whenever $A$ happens, $B$ happens. Then $B$ splits into $A$ and the part of $B$ outside $A$, written $B \setminus A$. Show that $P(A) \le P(B)$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Since $A \subseteq B$, $B$ is the union of $A$ and $B \setminus A$, which are disjoint.

hints.text: Which axiom turns a split into a sum?
The split must come before axiom 3 can add.
Split $B$, add with axiom 3, then drop a term that is at least 0.

feedback.correct: Split, add, then use that no chance is negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the split of $B$.

byKey.s3: The inequality needs the sum from axiom 3 first.

explain.text: $B$ is $A$ plus an extra piece, and that piece has chance at least 0. So $P(B)$ can only be larger than $P(A)$, or equal. This is **monotonicity**.

screens.title: Linda
screens.prose: Linda is 31, outspoken and very bright. She studied philosophy and campaigned against discrimination. Consider two statements. (a) Linda is a bank teller. (b) Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement.
screens.question: Which statement must be at least as probable as the other?

options.text: (a) Linda is a bank teller
(b) Linda is a bank teller and a feminist
options.why: The description fits a feminist, so (b) feels likely. But every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so (b) sits inside (a).

options.text: Neither: it depends on the description
options.why: The description moves both chances, but (b) always sits inside (a). No description can reverse that.

hints.text: Is every case of (b) also a case of (a)?
(b) is the shaded overlap; (a) is the whole bank teller circle.
$A \cap B \subseteq A$, so monotonicity gives $P(A \cap B) \le P(A)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the shaded overlap with the whole bank teller circle.

byKey.conj: The description fits a feminist, so (b) feels likely. But every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so (b) sits inside (a).

explain.text: Most people pick (b) when first asked: the **conjunction fallacy**. But (b) is the overlap, which lies inside (a). Monotonicity gives $P(A \cap B) \le P(A)$, however well the story fits.

screens.prose: Two events have $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.25$. Nobody tells you how much they overlap. Use monotonicity and inclusion and exclusion.
screens.question: Which values could $P(A \cup B)$ take? Select all that apply.

options.why: The union contains $A$, so by monotonicity it is at least $0.3$.
The union is at most $P(A) + P(B) = 0.55$, since the overlap term is at least 0.

hints.text: How small can the union be? It always contains $A$.
How large can it be? Inclusion and exclusion subtracts an overlap that is at least 0.
Anything from $0.3$, when $B$ sits inside $A$, up to $0.55$, when they are disjoint.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest and largest the union can be.

explain.text: The union contains $A$, so it is at least $0.3$. Inclusion and exclusion subtracts $P(A \cap B) \ge 0$, so it is at most $0.55$. That cap is the **union bound**: $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$.

screens.prose: From three axioms we derived: $$P(\emptyset) = 0, \qquad P(E^c) = 1 - P(E), \qquad 0 \le P(E) \le 1,$$ $$A \subseteq B \Rightarrow P(A) \le P(B), \qquad P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B).$$ One warning. A dart lands uniformly on $[0, 1]$, so an interval's chance is its length. One point has length 0.

state.caption: Chance of an interval = its length

screens.question: Is landing exactly on 0.5 impossible?

options.text: No. It can happen, but its probability is 0.
Yes. Probability 0 means it cannot happen.
options.why: With finitely many outcomes that is true. Here every point has probability 0, yet the dart lands somewhere.

options.text: No. Its probability is a tiny positive number.
options.why: Any tiny number fails: a shorter interval around 0.5 still contains it, and monotonicity caps the point's chance below that length.

feedback.correct: Probability 0 is not the same as impossible here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every single point has length 0, and the dart must land on one.

explain.text: By monotonicity the point's chance is at most any interval around it, however short. So it is 0, yet the dart always lands on some point. The course on random variables returns to this.

screens.prose: A risk report sets out three scenarios for next quarter. Exactly one will happen: recession 0.25, slowdown 0.40, growth 0.45.
screens.question: What is wrong with the report?

options.text: The scenarios are disjoint and cover every outcome, so their chances must add to 1.
Nothing: each number lies between 0 and 1.
options.why: Each number is fine alone. Disjoint scenarios covering everything must add to exactly 1, and these add to 1.1.

options.text: Nothing: scenarios can overlap, so the total may pass 1.
options.why: The report says exactly one scenario happens, so they are disjoint. Disjoint chances cannot add to more than 1.

options.text: Growth is too high and should be cut to 0.35.
options.why: The axioms cannot tell which number is wrong, only that the total is. Any fix needs the analyst's view.

hints.text: Exactly one scenario will happen. What does that say about the total?
Axioms 1 and 3 together force the total.
Disjoint scenarios that cover everything add to $P(S) = 1$.

feedback.correct: Axioms 1 and 3 force a total of 1; the report says 1.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three chances and compare with $P(S)$.

byKey.overlap: The report says exactly one scenario happens, so they are disjoint. Disjoint chances cannot add to more than 1.

explain.text: By axioms 3 and 1, disjoint scenarios covering everything add to $P(S) = 1$. A total of 1.1 means at least one number is too high. Any price or hedge built on these numbers inherits the error.

screens.prose: A trading firm runs 10 systems. Each fails on a given day with chance 0.002. Failures can be linked: a network outage can take several down at once.
screens.question: What upper limit does the union bound give for the chance that at least one system fails?

widget.label: Upper limit on the chance of any failure

hints.text: The union bound works for any number of events.
$P(E_1 \cup \dots \cup E_{10}) \le P(E_1) + \dots + P(E_{10})$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten chances.

byKey.one: That is one system. Any of the ten failing counts.
byKey.indep: $1 - 0.998^{10} \approx 0.0198$ assumes the failures are independent. The bound needs no such assumption.
byKey.all: That is the chance all ten fail at once, if independent. You want at least one.

explain.text: The union bound gives at most $10 \times 0.002 = 0.02$, whatever the links. Linked failures overlap, which only pulls the true chance below 0.02. That makes it a safe quick cap for risk limits.

ideas: Three axioms: the whole sample space has chance 1, no chance is negative, and disjoint chances add.
From them: $P(\emptyset) = 0$, $P(E^c) = 1 - P(E)$, $P(E) \le 1$, and a bigger event is at least as likely.
The union bound $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$ caps the chance of any failure, with no independence needed.

formula.name: Monotonicity
formula.note: So $P(A \cap B) \le P(A)$: “and” is never more likely than either part.

summary.trap: A detailed story can make “bank teller and feminist” feel likelier than “bank teller”. It never is: the overlap sits inside the circle.

quiz.prose: An analyst says: $P(\text{the stock falls more than } 5\%) = 0.4$ and $P(\text{the stock falls}) = 0.3$.
quiz.question: Can both numbers be right?

options.text: No: a fall of more than 5% is a fall, so its chance cannot be larger.
Yes: both are between 0 and 1.
options.why: Each is fine alone. But one event sits inside the other, so monotonicity orders them.

options.text: No: they add to 0.7, not 1.
options.why: The two events are not disjoint and do not cover everything, so they need not add to 1.

feedback.correct: Monotonicity: the smaller event cannot be more likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does one event sit inside the other?

explain.text: Every fall of more than 5% is a fall, so the first event is a subset of the second. Monotonicity forces $0.4 \le 0.3$, which is false. At least one number is wrong.

quiz.prose: Two disjoint events are given chances $P(A) = 0.45$ and $P(B) = 0.6$.
quiz.question: Is this possible?

options.text: No: axiom 3 would give $P(A \cup B) = 1.05$.
Yes: both chances are between 0 and 1.
options.why: Each is fine alone. But disjoint chances add, and the total passes 1.

options.text: Yes, as long as the overlap is 0.05.
options.why: Disjoint means the overlap is empty, so there is no 0.05 to take away.

feedback.correct: A union of disjoint events would have chance 1.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two chances with axiom 3.

explain.text: Axiom 3 gives $P(A \cup B) = 0.45 + 0.6 = 1.05$. But every chance is at most 1, so the numbers clash. Two disjoint events can share at most a total of 1.

quiz.prose: A model gives $P(\text{up today}) = 0.55$. It also gives $P(\text{up today and volume above average}) = 0.6$.
quiz.question: Which rule does the model break?

options.text: $P(A \cap B) \le P(A)$

options.why: No complement appears here. The issue is an “and” event beating one of its parts.

options.text: $P(A \cup B) \le P(A) + P(B)$
options.why: That bound is about “or”. Here an “and” event is larger than one of its parts.

options.text: No rule: the events are different
options.why: Different events, but one sits inside the other. That orders their chances.

feedback.correct: An “and” event lies inside each of its parts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the “and” event with “up today”.

explain.text: Up with high volume is a subset of up. Monotonicity gives $P(A \cap B) \le P(A)$, so 0.6 cannot exceed 0.55. This is the Linda trap in a trading model.

quiz.prose: Five strategies each breach their loss limit on a given day with chance 0.01. Breaches may be linked.
quiz.question: What upper limit does the union bound give for the chance that at least one breaches?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the five chances.

byKey.one: That is one strategy. Any of the five counts.
byKey.indep: $1 - 0.99^5 \approx 0.049$ assumes independence. The bound does not need it.

explain.text: The union bound gives $P(\text{any}) \le 5 \times 0.01 = 0.05$. It holds however the breaches are linked. Overlap only lowers the true value.
